drug_class: Biologic DMARD (Disease-Modifying Antirheumatic Drug) / TNF inhibitor
purpose: Etanercept is used to treat conditions where your immune system attacks your own body, such as rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, plaque psoriasis, and juvenile idiopathic arthritis. It helps reduce pain, swelling, and joint damage. It can also help clear up skin plaques in people with psoriasis.
how_it_works: Your body makes a protein called TNF (tumor necrosis factor) that causes inflammation. In some diseases, your body makes too much TNF, which leads to painful swelling and damage. Etanercept acts like a sponge — it binds to and blocks that extra TNF before it can cause harm, helping calm down your overactive immune system.
common_side_effects: The most common side effect is redness, itching, swelling, or pain at the injection site where you give yourself the shot. You may also notice headaches, stomach upset, or a runny nose. Some people get minor skin rashes.
warnings: Because etanercept lowers your immune system, it makes it harder for your body to fight infections — so you are at higher risk for serious infections including tuberculosis (TB). Tell your doctor right away if you have a fever, chills, cough, or feel very unwell. You should NOT take this medication if you have an active infection. It may also increase the risk of certain cancers, and you should avoid live vaccines while taking it. Always tell all your doctors and your pharmacist that you are on this medication.
typical_dosing: Etanercept is given as an injection under the skin (subcutaneous). For most adults with rheumatoid arthritis or psoriatic arthritis, the typical dose is 50 mg once a week. For plaque psoriasis, it may start at 50 mg twice a week for 3 months, then drop to once a week. Your doctor will decide the right dose for your condition. It comes as a prefilled syringe or auto-injector pen to make self-injection easier at home.
